question:
A 36-year-old woman comes to the physician because she has not had her menstrual period for the past 4 months. During this period, she has had frequent headaches, difficulty sleeping, and increased sweating. She has not had any weight changes. Over the past year, menses occurred at irregular 30- to 45-day intervals with light flow. The patient underwent two successful cesarean sections at the ages of 28 and 32. She has two healthy children. She is sexually active with her husband and does not use condoms. Her vital signs are within normal limits. Physical examination shows no abnormalities. Laboratory studies show:
Estradiol 8 pg/mL (mid-follicular phase: N=27–123 pg/mL)
Follicle-stimulating hormone 200 mIU/mL
Luteinizing hormone 180 mIU/mL
Prolactin 16 ng/mL
Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?"?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Elevated follicle-stimulating hormone (FSH) -> Elevated luteinizing hormone (LH) -> Low estradiol levels -> Premature ovarian failure -> opc. Premature ovarian failure -> 80%
CHAIN: Absence of weight changes -> Exclusion of pregnancy -> Elevated FSH and LH levels -> Premature ovarian failure -> opc. Premature ovarian failure -> 85%
CHAIN: History of irregular menstrual cycles -> Low estradiol levels -> Elevated FSH and LH levels -> Premature ovarian failure -> opc. Premature ovarian failure -> 75%
enhanced_information: The most likely diagnosis for the 36-year-old woman with elevated FSH, LH, and low estradiol levels is premature ovarian failure. This is supported by the patient's history of irregular menstrual cycles, absence of weight changes ruling out pregnancy, and the laboratory findings. The evidence path confirming the association between LH and premature menopause further supports this diagnosis.
analysis: The patient's presentation of irregular menstrual cycles, elevated FSH and LH levels, and low estradiol levels is highly suggestive of premature ovarian failure. This is further supported by her symptoms and history of successful pregnancies. Pregnancy is unlikely due to the absence of weight changes and the laboratory findings. Other options like primary hypothyroidism, polycystic ovary syndrome, and major depressive disorder do not align well with the clinical picture and lab results.
